name: Print In Range
html:
Welcome Back Reader!

We hope that you are getting the concepts of Binary Search Tree so far.

Moving further, in this article we will discuss about the next problem on the BST i.e. Print In Range.

So we can get a hint from the name of the problem that we need to print all the values of a given Binary Tree which lies in the given range.

Before you move any further, it is advised that you give this problem a fair try.


Important Links : Problem Link, Question Video , Solution Video

Let's jump to the problem.

Problem Discussion :

In this problem you are given a partially written BST class.

All you have to do is to complete the body of the "pir" function. The function is expected to print all nodes between d1 and d2 (inclusive and increasing order).

Input and Output is managed for you.

If you are finding it difficult to understand then we recommend you to watch the question video of this topic. I am sure that question will get much clearer once you watch it.

Watch video Approach :

The problem here deals with printing of all the nodes in ascending sorted order which is in the range of d1 and d2.

  • First of all, we must get to our conclusion that the required result should be in ascendingly sorted order henceforth we shall apply inorder in some way here.
  • As we are given a BST therefore we can discard subtree(s) by checking whether the given range lies in the left subtree or right subtree.
  • If the range can lie in both the subtrees then we shall consider both the subtrees by applying the inorder traversal as it would ensure the relative sorting of elements.

Let's understand above points using an example:

Consider the BST given below and suppose you need to print all the elements within the range of (27 - 72):

  • So first of all we check whether 50 lies in range or not. Yes! It does lie in the range therefore, we need to travel to both the children of 50.
  • And as mentioned above, this traveling will be done using inorder traversal.
  • Following inorder traversal, we first reach the left of 50 which is 25.
  • Now we check whether 25 is in the given range or not. No It's not. And as 25 is smaller than given range, so it means that the only possibility to find an element within range in 25's subtree is by moving to it's right branch.
  • 37 is present on the right of 25. And also it is in the given range. So it implies that calls will be made to both the children. Of course, first to the left one. On the left, 30 is present which is again in range.
  • Therefore, further calls will be made to both its children. First left of 30 is visited. But since it's left is null, the control returns to 30 itself. Now 30 gets printed. And 30's right is called. Which is again null, returning the control finally to 37.
  • Now 37 gets printed. And 37's right, 40 is called.
  • First left of 40 is visited. But since it's left is null, the control returns to 40 itself. Now 40 gets printed. And 40's right is called. Which is again null, returning the control finally to 37.
  • 37 returns the control to 25 and 25 returns it to 50.
  • At 50, 50 is printed and now 50's right 75 is called.
  • Now we check whether 75 is in the given range or not. No It's not. And as 75 is greater than the given range, it means that the only possibility to find an element within range in 75's subtree is by moving to it's left branch.
  • 62 is present on the right of 75. And also it is in the given range. So it implies that calls will be made to both the children. Of course, first to the left one. On the left, 60 is present which is again in range.
  • Therefore, further calls will be made to both its children. First left of 60 is visited. But since it's left is null, the control returns to 60 itself. Now 60 gets printed. And 60's right is called. Which is again null, returning the control finally to 62.
  • Now 62 gets printed. And 37's right, 70 is called.
  • First left of 70 is visited. But since it's left is null, the control returns to 70 itself. Now 40 gets printed. And 70's right is called. Which is again null, returning the control finally to 62.
  • 62 returns the control to 75 and 75 returns it to 50.

To summarize:

  • We are simply applying inorder traversal in this problem.
  • And for every subtree, we are keeping a check to avoid visiting redundant subtrees that are out of range to make our code more efficient.

Let's try to code this:

Yes, that looks perfect!!

import java.io.*; import java.util.*; public class Main { public static class Node { int data; Node left; Node right; Node(int data, Node left, Node right) { this.data = data; this.left = left; this.right = right; } } public static class Pair { Node node; int state; Pair(Node node, int state) { this.node = node; this.state = state; } } public static Node construct(Integer[] arr) { Node root = new Node(arr[0], null, null); Pair rtp = new Pair(root, 1); Stack< Pair> st = new Stack< >(); st.push(rtp); int idx = 0; while (st.size() > 0) { Pair top = st.peek(); if (top.state == 1) { idx++; if (arr[idx] != null) { top.node.left = new Node(arr[idx], null, null); Pair lp = new Pair(top.node.left, 1); st.push(lp); } else { top.node.left = null; } top.state++; } else if (top.state == 2) { idx++; if (arr[idx] != null) { top.node.right = new Node(arr[idx], null, null); Pair rp = new Pair(top.node.right, 1); st.push(rp); } else { top.node.right = null; } top.state++; } else { st.pop(); } } return root; } public static void display(Node node) { if (node == null) { return; } String str = ""; str += node.left == null ? "." : node.left.data + ""; str += " <- " + node.data + " -> "; str += node.right == null ? "." : node.right.data + ""; System.out.println(str); display(node.left); display(node.right); } public static void pir(Node node, int d1, int d2) { if (node == null) { return; } if (node.data > d1 && node.data > d2) { pir(node.left, d1, d2); } else if (node.data < d1 && node.data < d2) { pir(node.right, d1, d2); } else { pir(node.left, d1, d2); System.out.println(node.data); pir(node.right, d1, d2); } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(System.in)); int n = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); Integer[] arr = new Integer[n]; String[] values = br.readLine().split(" "); for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (values[i].equals("n") == false) { arr[i] = Integer.parseInt(values[i]); } else { arr[i] = null; } } int d1 = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); int d2 = Integer.parseInt(br.readLine()); Node root = construct(arr); pir(root, d1, d2); } }
java; true"; Analysis Time Complexity:

O(logn)

The time complexity for the function is proportional to the height of the binary search tree as for every call we are neglecting one of the subtrees.

Space Complexity:

O(logn)

The space complexity for the function is proportional to the height of the tree due to the recursion stack.
